title: Negotiating Gender and Justice

extra.summary: Long neglected and marginalized by the state, inhabitants of Turkey’s southeast region, particularly its Kurdish communities, look not to the official courts but to renowned local figures, religious leaders, and civil organizations to resolve disputes. This paper explores three types of alternative judicial bodies (AJBs): (1) traditional Heqî AJBs, which prioritize religion and patriarchy in their decision-making; (2) self-identified progressive AJBs run by local civil society organizations; and (3) newly emerging AJBs aligned with state institutions, reflecting the state’s new frontiers in the region. Although these judicial bodies, shaped by diverse adjudicative tendencies and deeply embedded in the region’s religious, political, and social fabric, differ in their impact in terms of whom and what they include or exclude, they collectively provide alternative pathways for dispute resolution. This paper examines the role of AJBs in resolving disputes in the Kurdish southeast, focusing on gender, religious discourses, the involvement of feminist activists and organizations, and the positionality of these bodies within regional politics and sovereignty formation. Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Mardin, it examines interactions between Kurdish AJBs and women’s agency and mobility, while situating AJBs within broader debates on legal pluralism and gender justice in feminist legal scholarship.

title: The Diaspora of Pre-Columbian Objects from Atacama into a Global Network of Goods, Collectors, and Museums between 1850 and 1950

extra.summary: Pre-Columbian objects from Atacama not only held value and articulated social relations in pre-European times. To this day, and from at least the nineteenth century onward, they continue to play this role by being exhibited in national and international museum showcases, reproduced in catalogs, or owned by private collectors. It is clear that their past value was changed in these new contexts, but what did not change was their amazing ability to bring individuals and institutions together across time and space, even across continents and generations. The bonds forged in the acquisition, circulation, and possession of these ancient objects and collections formed a global network of relationships between humans and things. Such a web was not woven randomly or whimsically but rather warped within the structure of the world system where the Atacama Desert has participated since the mid-nineteenth century, orchestrated principally by the saltpeter, copper, industrial, and mercantile economies. The circulation and biographies of pre-Columbian objects from Atacama is an extraordinary source for understanding the world system in which they were extracted, exchanged, accumulated, assembled, inherited, and exhibited between 1850 and 1950. This dual reflection also opens up a fantastic possibility to better comprehend the role of the cultural works of the past in the making of each social reality at different moments in time.

title: An Archaeology of Redress

extra.summary: Black studies critical theorizations have much to offer the field of archaeology both in theory and in practice. For Saidiya Hartman, redress entails confronting formations of epistemic violence that undergird the archival record; it is a praxis that is always incomplete. This article maps Hartman’s theory of redress onto the practice of community archaeology to explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when archaeologists center youth engagement, capacity building, and cultural and natural heritage stewardship. Using the Estate Little Princess Archaeology Project as a case study, we explore one way archaeologists attempt to offer restitution to the issues their work reveals (i.e., legacies of environmental racism, truncated avenues of economic sustainability, racialized disenfranchisement) through an “archaeology of redress.”

title: Middle-class locations: emplacements and displacements of habitus among the French in London
affiliation: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

extra.summary: This article examines the alterations of habitus that lead to feelings of emplacement and displacement among middle-class French citizens living in London. I broaden Bourdieu’s concept of split habitus, developed primarily in the context of social mobility, and extend it to questions of geographic mobility. I characterize the French in London as “sideways migrants” who move to a nearby nation with comparable socio-economic indicators and global standing, seeking to maintain their middle-class status through transversal mobility. They are “nation straddlers” who experience dislocations of habitus shaped in the French national social space after relocating to London. I present the cases of four French women in London, drawing upon a larger longitudinal ethnographic study, to expand understandings of how migrant aspirations and practices are connected to the positionality of habitus in both the social space of the nation of origin and that of resettlement. Migration research that situates migrants in national social spaces that they straddle, as in the case of sideways migrants, has important implications for broader questions about the durability and nature of both class and national identity in the contemporary world.

title: Nationalism, Balance of Power, and World Order: Untangling Neorealism's Troubled Relationship With Nationalism

extra.summary: ABSTRACT While many explain the crisis of the liberal international order through nationalism, its treatment by neorealist scholars remains frustrating. Untangling the nationalism–neorealism relationship would help explain the current crisis and enhance neorealism's explanatory power. First, this article reviews and critically assesses neorealist scholarship (defensive, offensive and neoclassical realism) about nationalism. Then, using these insights, I propose a distinctively neorealist theory of nationalism. International power shifts reshape nationalism, which, in turn, conditions the behaviour and discourse of the great powers. Rising material capabilities foster offensive nationalism; diminishing capabilities foster defensive nationalism. Hence, global power shifts—foremost the United States' decline relative to China and Russia—transformed the great powers' nationalism, breaking the post‐Cold War order. This approach enables predictions about nationalism's future. If the global power distribution stabilises, the ‘distribution’ of nationalism should stabilise, too; the evolution of nationalism shows a degree of predictability. Pursuing a ‘neorealist nationalism’ research agenda helps tackle fundamental questions about the international order.

title: Infrastructure nationalism and sovereignty by settlement in Tibet: The case of xiaokang border villages

extra.summary: This article critically examines China’s Xiaokang Border Village Programme (2017–20) in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), situating it within Xi Jinping’s broader strategy of ‘governing the borders to govern the country’. Ostensibly framed as a poverty alleviation and rural revitalization initiative, the programme mobilized billions in state funding to construct or rebuild more than 600 model villages in Tibet’s border counties. Drawing on a range of new sources, the article argues that these villages are less developmental tools than instruments of territorial consolidation, securitization, and ideological transformation. By reconfiguring spatial relations, relocating border populations, and embedding Han-led Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, these xiaokang villages function as micro-sites of infrastructure nationalism and colonial-style governance, inscribing Han norms into Indigenous landscapes and subjectivities to further CCP control over once autonomous communities in the farthest reaches of the People’s Republic of China.

title: Globalizing the Tribal Culture, Landscapes and Customary Practices Through Indigenous Tourism
affiliation: Central Tribal University of Andhra Pradesh; Andhra Pradesh Forest Department

extra.summary: The world today is focusing on the concept of inclusivity and holistic development. The indigenous communities are at the edge of it to ensure the integrated growth of man and nature. They are critical for fostering well-being of humankind through sustainable practices. India is home to 104.2 million indigenous people of the world and the second largest indigenous territory after China. These indigenous people are rich in their rituals, customary practices and their age-old knowledge systems. They have passed on their knowledge from one generation to another for ages orally; however, lack of documentation has resulted in their cultural loss. It includes various cultural elements such as dance, music, painting, fairs, festivals, storytelling, puppetry and so on. Especially, in the era of globalization, when the cultural homogenization is taking place at a faster pace due to the effect of digitalization and modernization, the traditional artefacts of tribes are vanishing quickly. This research article thus tries to document various unique cultural footprints of tribes from different parts of the country. The article particularly focuses on the scope and role of indigenous tourism, which plays an important role in familiarizing various cultural regimes to tribal landscapes and enhances the process of glocalization, that is, global to local. This can further boost the tribal economy as well as acquaint tribal material culture to the world.

title: A culturally tailored Zhuang embroidery intervention for psychological well-being among Zhuang adults in the retirement transition in Guangxi: a waitlist-controlled quasi-experimental study

extra.summary: Background Arts- and craft-based community programs may support psychological well-being in later life, yet few studies have examined culturally tailored ethnic heritage crafts as public health interventions in their communities of origin. Methods This waitlist-controlled quasi-experimental study evaluated an eight-week intervention integrating Zhuang embroidery practice, cultural storytelling, and group exchange among community-dwelling Zhuang adults aged 55–65 years in Guangxi, China. Eighty participants were allocated by community cluster to intervention or waitlist control groups and assessed at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 12-week follow-up. Psychological well-being was the primary outcome; loneliness, social connectedness, general well-being, ethnic identity, process perception, and qualitative interview findings were secondary or exploratory materials. Results The intervention group showed greater immediate improvement in Ryff psychological well-being than waitlist controls. Baseline-adjusted sensitivity analysis supported the immediate Ryff signal, whereas the follow-up difference was attenuated. title: Coupling Mechanism and Driving Paths of the Spatial Differentiation of Tourism Attractions from the Perspective of Tourist Perception—A Case Study of Xinjiang, China
affiliation: Xinjiang University; Guangdong-Hongkong-Macau Joint Laboratory of Collaborative Innovation for Environmental Quality; Guangzhou Urban Planning Survey & Design Institute; Sun Yat-sen University

extra.summary: As the culture and tourism industry moves toward high-quality development, tourist perception has become a core dimension for measuring that quality. Most existing work on tourism spatial differentiation still looks at the supply side, and describes the pattern of tourism attractions. It pays limited attention to how supply and demand couple with each other, and it offers little systematic evidence from large-scale, highly heterogeneous regions. This study combines multi-source tourism point data with review texts from Trip.com (hereafter, Trip) and Rednote (Xiaohongshu). Using RoBERTa-wwm, a pretrained Chinese language model with whole-word masking, together with a coupling-coordination model and the geographical detector, we analyze how the spatial differentiation of tourism attractions couples with tourist perception, and we trace the driving mechanism to land resources, tourism resources and socioeconomic conditions. The results show that tourist sentiment perception in Xinjiang forms a spatial pattern that is led by core cities and declines outward layer by layer, and the coupling coordination between the distribution of tourism attractions and tourist sentiment perception remains higher in the north and lower in the south. The two systems do not, however, follow a simple linear relation: infrastructure coverage emerges as the strongest correlate of coordination, whereas regional economy and population size explain it only weakly. title: Climate Extremes, Demographic Restructuring, and Population Exposure in Xinjiang: Potential Socio-Cultural Implications in a Multi-Ethnic Arid Region
affiliation: Yunnan University; GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences

extra.summary: Extreme climate change and demographic change jointly reshape human exposure in arid and culturally diverse regions. This study examines projected changes in climate extremes and population exposure in Xinjiang, China, during 2021–2100 under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5 (SSP5-8.5). An ensemble of eight models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) was used to assess very wet-day precipitation (R95p), warm days (TX90p), and consecutive dry days (CDD), while gridded total-population projections were combined with provincial-level age- and education-specific demographic projections. Comparing the late-century period (2081–2100) with the early-century baseline (2021–2040), ensemble-mean R95p increases by approximately 47%, TX90p by 167%, and CDD decreases by about 9.9%. Population remains concentrated in oasis cities and piedmont zones, with urbanization increasing from 49.6% to 77.0%. Demographic restructuring substantially changes the composition of exposure: the elderly share rises from 9.3% to 39.4%, producing the fastest increase in age-specific exposure, while the highly educated population expands from 5.5% to 48.6%. The analysis identifies spatiotemporal concurrence rather than causal effects of climate on migration and should be interpreted as an exposure-oriented assessment rather than a complete vulnerability analysis. title: Built Heritage Perception and Spatial Patterns of Tourist Affect in Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture, China: A Social Media–Based Assessment
affiliation: Ningbo University; Huazhong University of Science and Technology

extra.summary: Against the backdrop of the concurrent processes of tourism development, spatial commercialisation, and architectural heritage conservation, identifying tourists’ cognitive images of destinations and differences in textual valence provides an important basis for evaluating the quality of tourism built environments and implementing fine-grained spatial governance. Taking Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture in Yunnan Province as the study area, this study analyses 32,992 Ctrip attraction reviews using high-frequency term identification, two-level theoretical coding, a semantic co-occurrence network, and affective analysis to construct an attraction-level image-affect analytical framework. The results show that, under a theory-guided codebook, review content can be organised into four dimensions: natural landscapes, built heritage, ethnic culture, and services and accessibility. Natural mountain–lake scenery has the broadest review coverage, while strong semantic associations among architectural character, Bai vernacular dwellings, and Bai culture indicate that built heritage is an important spatial representation through which tourists recognise local culture. Textual valence is predominantly positive: positive, neutral, and negative affective terms account for 71.87%, 22.65%, and 5.48%, respectively. title: The spatio-temporal pattern and influencing factors of toponymic cultural heritage in Ningxia
affiliation: Ocean University of China; Qingdao University; Chinese Academy of Sciences; Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research

extra.summary: Toponymic cultural heritage (TCH) forms a critical yet often undervalued layer of cultural landscapes, encapsulating historical human-environment interactions. Despite growing focus on heritage conservation, a significant research gap persists: there is limited empirical evidence on how TCH spatial clustering evolves across historical periods and what specific environmental and socio-demographic thresholds drive its concentration, hindering the development of temporally and spatially nuanced conservation strategies. Addressing this gap, this study analyzes the spatio-temporal patterns and drivers of TCH across 22 county-level units in Ningxia, China. Spatial autocorrelation analysis (Global Moran’s I) reveals significant positive spatial dependence with a pulsed pattern of alternating weak and strong agglomeration over time. Peak clustering occurred between the Qin-Han and Song-Yuan dynasties. The distribution is shaped by an interplay of natural and social factors; an optimal ‘moderate zone’ characterized by a relative height difference of 500–1000 m, a river network density of 50–150 m/km2, and a contemporary Hui population below 500,000 fosters the highest concentration of culturally significant toponyms.
